items.title: Abnormal starts
items.lede: In AUTO the PMU should terminate the sequence if it detects a no start or projects a hung or hot start. "Should" is the word to hold on to: the abort criteria are still yours to judge, and NATOPS lists five situations in which you abort the start manually whatever the PMU is doing.

items.title: Aborted takeoff
items.lede: If it becomes necessary to abort the takeoff, concentrate on maintaining aircraft control, specifically directional control, while stopping the aircraft on the remaining runway.

items.title: Accelerated stall

numbers.label: Do not sustain heavy buffet above

items.lede: A stall at a G loading above one, so at a speed well above the one-G stall speed. Under two G there is little buffet before it happens; above two, airframe buffet precedes the stall and is the warning. The recognisable part is the roll-off: from a turning entry the stall shows as an abrupt lateral roll.

items.title: Acceleration limitations

references.loc: §901 — Rules and Precautions for Aerobatic Flight

items.lede: Four numbers for load factor and three for how long you may sit at low or negative G. The pattern in the four is that everything gets smaller: dirty is smaller than clean, and rolling is smaller than symmetric.

items.title: Aerobatic maneuvers

references.loc: §901 — Rules and Precautions for Aerobatic Flight
§4.4 — Unusual Attitude, Stalls, and Spin Training

items.lede: Nine maneuvers built out of three ideas: a pull in the vertical, a roll about the longitudinal axis, and a combination of the two. What separates them at the brief table is entry airspeed and power, and what separates them in the air is where the nose stops.

items.title: Aileron roll
items.lede: A 360° roll about the longitudinal axis, complete when the wings are back parallel to the horizon. The simplest of the set, and the one where control inputs are smooth, brisk and positive rather than gentle.

items.title: Airborne-damaged aircraft

references.loc: Ch. 3 — Controllability Check (Structural Damage/Flight Control Malfunction)

items.lede: If a bird strike, structural damage, or a flight control malfunction occurs or is suspected in flight, a decision to abandon the aircraft or attempt a landing must be made. The Controllability Check aids the pilot in determining whether the aircraft may be safely landed, and if so, what configuration is best for safe landing. A mid-air collision is an inherent risk when flying formation. Mid-air collisions can be either minimal or catastrophic and can be within the section or external to the flight.

items.title: Aircraft and cockpit lighting
items.lede: The landing and taxi lights are on the gear and only illuminate with all gear down and locked, which makes them a gear indication as well as a light. Everything else is ordinary. Night mode selected in either cockpit puts the displays in both cockpits into night mode.

items.title: Aircraft departs prepared surface

references.loc: Ch. 3 — Emergency Engine Shutdown on the Ground
Ch. 3 — Landing With Blown Main Tire

items.lede: If it appears likely that the aircraft will depart the prepared surface, execute the Emergency Engine Shutdown On The Ground procedure.

items.title: Aircraft discrepancy reporting

references.loc: §3.12 — Degraded Integrated Avionics Computer Mitigation Procedures
§3.2 — Actual Emergencies and Precautionary Emergency Landings

items.lede: A flight that executes an emergency procedure, that is terminated by a malfunction requiring a precautionary emergency landing, or that is terminated by an aircrew illness requiring medical attention is reported to the ODO, who notifies the CO, XO, OPSO, Safety Officer and the TW-4 Command Duty Officer. Which report is written afterwards is set by each squadron.

items.title: Aircraft issue

references.loc: §3.12 — Degraded Integrated Avionics Computer Mitigation Procedures

items.lede: Aircrew verify side number and parking spot in maintenance control and verbally confirm with the other crew member before opening the canopy. A degraded integrated avionics computer decides whether the aircraft is taken at all.

items.title: Airfield and runway lighting

references.loc: Section B §7 — Pilot Control of Airport Lighting
Section B §6 — Wave-Off Lighting at USN/USMC Airports

items.lede: Blue lights mark all taxiways, white lights mark the boundaries of the duty runway, green lights mark the threshold of the duty runway, and red lights mark all obstructions on the airfield. A rotating white and green beacon is located at fields that are open for night operations.

items.title: Airspace classification
items.lede: The AIM defines controlled airspace as "a generic term that covers the different classifications of airspace (Class A, B, C, D, and E) and defined dimensions within which air traffic control service is provided to IFR and VFR flights in accordance with the airspace classification." When flying a visual navigation route under VFR, visibility and cloud clearance requirements are different in controlled and uncontrolled airspace.

items.title: Airspeed changes
items.lede: Smooth, controlled, deliberate change of airspeed is an integral part of instrument flying. Change airspeed while maintaining heading and altitude. Power is used to initiate the change, and at the completion of the change power is set to maintain the new airspeed. The aircraft should be trimmed during airspeed changes and then fine-tuned once the target airspeed is achieved. This maneuver is normally practiced between 150 and 200 KIAS, and the Power-Attitude-Trim principle applies.

items.title: Airway navigation
items.lede: Flying the published route structure means always knowing which NAVAID you are navigating on and when you stop. That swap is the changeover point, and how you find it depends on what defines the fix — DME gives you a number, two radials make you share one receiver between two stations.

items.title: Aldis lamp signals
items.lede: The light gun is how tower talks to an aircraft with no radio. Acknowledge by day with aileron or rudder movement on the ground and by rocking the wings in the air; acknowledge at night by flashing the aircraft lights. A signal you do not acknowledge is a signal tower has to assume you did not see.

items.title: Alternate filing minimums
items.lede: Whether you need an alternate, and what weather it has to be forecast to have, is decided by the destination forecast for the hour either side of ETA. Three rows. The one worth having cold is the middle one, because the answer depends on whether the alternate’s approach is precision or non-precision.

items.title: Anti-spin recovery procedures

references.loc: Ch. 3 — Inadvertent Departure from Controlled Flight

items.lede: Recover from a steady state spin by using NATOPS erect spin recovery procedures. Apply full rudder opposite to the direction of turn needle, follow immediately with smooth, positive forward stick to a position forward of neutral, and do not use ailerons.

items.title: Any maneuver performed in this block

events.title: Day Familiarization
events.label: any maneuver performed in this block

items.lede: A full local area profile flown from the maneuvers already introduced, in sequence. The list below is generated from the syllabus: every maneuver briefed by an earlier event in this stage.
terms: Any maneuver performed in this block

items.title: AOA approach
items.lede: A descending 180° balanced turn to final followed by a normal flared landing, flown to optimum angle of attack rather than to an airspeed. Attitude holds the AOA and power holds the rate of descent. It is an AOA approach, not an AOA landing.

items.title: Approach maneuver
items.lede: In addition to developing basic airwork scan and trim skills, the Approach Pattern incorporates many of the basic skill sets required during execution of a Low Altitude Instrument Approach from over a NAVAID. It runs two minutes of timing, a 210° turn, three 1000 foot descents, two of them at 120 KIAS in the Basic Approach Configuration, and a missed approach.

items.title: Arc-radial intercepts
items.lede: Turn off an arc to establish the aircraft on a radial, inbound or outbound, to the NAVAID. During some approaches, missed approaches and departure procedures you will be required to fly an arc and then intercept a radial from that arc. In this situation you need to calculate a lead radial at which to start your turn off the arc to intercept the radial.

items.title: Arcing approach
items.lede: An arcing approach makes use of an arcing maneuver to position the aircraft inbound on an intermediate or final approach course. Arcing approaches are normally identified by VOR/DME or TACAN in the approach plate margin, indicating DME is required.

items.title: Arcing
items.lede: Arcing is defined as flying at a constant distance from a NAVAID by referencing DME from that station. Arcing about a NAVAID may be required to comply with an ATC clearance and is an integral part of many approaches, departure procedures, and arrivals. In practice, you do not actually fly a perfect arc, but by varying AOB and heading, a close approximation of an arc can be achieved.

items.title: Area and sun management
items.lede: The Formation Lead will keep the flight within the proper operating area and clear of clouds and other aircraft. As Lead, it is important to take the sun into consideration while maneuvering the flight. During early morning flights and late afternoon flights, particularly in the winter months, the sun is lower in the sky and will be more of a factor.

items.title: ASR approach

references.loc: §907 — Airport Surveillance Approach (ASR) and PAR Without Glideslope (PAR W/O GS)

items.lede: During the ASR approach, the controller utilizes an airport surveillance radar system to transition the aircraft to the runway environment. This controller can only provide course and range information. Because no glideslope information is available, it constitutes a non-precision approach.

items.title: Avionics failures

references.loc: Ch. 3 — MFD Failure or Avionics Bus Failure
Ch. 3 — Backup Flight Instrument Display Failure

items.lede: During all electronic display failures, the pilot should confirm indications in both cockpits, if occupied, reference alternate data sources or the backup instruments as applicable, and check applicable circuit breakers.

items.title: Avionics malfunctions
items.lede: Nearly every avionics failure starts the same way: reference the BFI, check the circuit breaker, and confirm the indication in the other cockpit. The last of those is the diagnostic. A failure that appears in one cockpit and not the other is a different problem from one that appears in both.

items.title: Barrel roll

references.loc: §902 — Section Lines and Ground Reference Points

items.lede: A Barrel Roll is a maneuver in which the aircraft is rolled 360° about an imaginary point which bears 45° off the nose of the aircraft. Definite seat pressure should be felt throughout the roll. Practice in both directions.

items.title: Basic air work
items.lede: Basic Air Work is one of the items graded on all complete syllabus events. The behavior statement is to establish and maintain desired altitude, airspeed and heading during flight.

items.title: Basic transitions
items.lede: Basic transitions are used to initiate or level off from a climb or descent. The four basic transitions are climb-to-cruise, cruise-to-climb, cruise-to-descent, and descent-to-cruise. Use the P.A.T. principle to make all transitions.

items.title: Battery and generator failure
items.lede: This checklist assumes that the generator has failed and the main battery is totally depleted. The only operative instruments with auxiliary battery power will be the backup flight instrument, fire detection system (FIRE 1 only), IRU, and VHF radio, with tuning provided by the standby VHF control head.

items.title: Battery bus light during start
items.lede: The engine start should be aborted manually if the red BATT BUS warning message illuminates during the start sequence.

items.title: BFI approach
items.lede: Maneuver the aircraft by means of the backup flight instrument only. With a loss of inputs from the Air Data Computer, the Internal Reference Unit, or in the event of a dual Integrated Avionics Computer failure with total loss of all MFDs, the Primary Flight Display may be lost or rendered unusable; however, flight may be continued and aircraft attitude controlled by referring to the BFI.

items.title: Backup flight instrument
items.lede: The backup flight instrument is located in the upper right side of the instrument panel in each cockpit and provides attitude, altitude, airspeed, heading and vertical velocity. This instrument provides backup indications in the event of failure of the electronic flight instrumentation system or the aircraft electrical system.

items.title: Blind procedures
items.lede: Blind is the term used to communicate that visual contact is lost with a member of the formation while maneuvering in VMC. In the event Wing loses sight of Lead in VMC, Wing will immediately call "(TAC call sign), blind, (altitude)". The visual aircraft has de-confliction responsibility.

items.title: Blindfold cockpit check
items.lede: A special syllabus requirement on FAM2101. The SNA demonstrates a safe knowledge of the location of eleven controls.

items.title: Brake failure
items.lede: If landing with a known wheel brake failure in one wheel, land on the side of the runway corresponding to the failed brake. If landing with a known brake failure in both wheels, plan for a firm, on-speed touchdown in the center of the runway.

items.title: Brief and debrief

references.loc: Ch. I §7 — Ground Training and Briefing Requirements

items.lede: The pilot in command should give a preflight briefing for all participating flight crew and ground crew members, if applicable, regarding mission plan and individual responsibilities. The NATOPS list of briefing items is a recommendation of the minimum information a preflight briefing should include, and is not meant to replace local guidelines. After each event, the instructor critiques the student performance using cause and effect analysis, particularly with respect to the CTS.

items.title: CDI reverse sensing precautions
items.lede: Normal CDI sensing will be available only if the front course is set into the CDI. The front course is the final approach course depicted for the ILS or LOC approach procedure. On approaches titled LOC BC the depicted FAC is the back course and will result in reverse sensing if set into the CDI.

items.title: CFS and ejection CRM
items.lede: The aircraft uses a dual redundant canopy fracturing system to provide a clear path for the pilots during ejection or emergency ground egress. The CFS has two modes of operation: automatic initiation during ejection, and manual initiation by the internal CFS initiators.

items.title: Change of route or destination

events.title: Instrument Navigation
events.label: change of flight plan while airborne

items.lede: Refiling airborne. Thirteen items in a fixed order, printed on the inside back cover of the IFR Supplement, and the reason to know they are there is that you will be reading them out while flying the aircraft. Have the page open before you key the mic.
terms: change of flight plan while airborne

items.title: Checklist challenge-action response format

references.loc: §2 — How to Use This Checklist Guide

items.lede: The checklists will be conducted in the challenge-action-response format. This means you report the **challenge**, accomplish the required **action**, and state the appropriate **response**. As you check each item, place your hand on the item to ensure the desired position is selected.

items.title: Chip detector warning
items.lede: Illumination of the CHIP warning indicates possible metal contamination in the engine oil supply. If the contamination is severe, the engine may fail with little or no further warning.

items.title: Circling maneuver
items.lede: Breaking out of an approach that does not line up with the runway you are landing on, and maneuvering visually to one that does. Form the plan before you start the approach, stay at or above the circling altitude until you are in a position to land, and know the missed approach — because losing sight while circling is what the whole procedure guards against.

items.title: Clearance and departure procedures
items.lede: Once you have filed an IFR flight plan, ATC will approve, disapprove, or revise your plan and provide it to the appropriate controlling agency. An instrument departure is a procedure used to ensure a safe climb out from an airport and to provide safe separation between aircraft. There are four common types of departure.

items.title: Cloud clearances
items.lede: The flight visibility and distance from clouds required to remain VFR, set by altitude band and by whether the airspace is controlled or uncontrolled.

items.title: Combination maneuvers
items.lede: A Combination Maneuver is nothing more than combining a series of aerobatic maneuvers into a single evolution. A maximum of four maneuvers may be linked together. All maneuvers are performed in accordance with the procedures previously set forth for the maneuvers you intend to fly.

items.title: Constant airspeed climbs and descents
items.lede: Practice maintaining heading and airspeed during climbs and descents. This maneuver will be flown using the same airspeed, power settings and nose attitudes as the Vertical S-1 Pattern. The objective is to stress the concept of using nose attitude to control airspeed during climbs and descents while practicing basic scan and trim skills.

items.title: Contact unusual attitudes

references.loc: §4.4 — Unusual Attitude, Stalls, and Spin Training

items.lede: Recovery from an attitude you did not intend: an improperly flown maneuver, disorientation, an area boundary, a malfunction, a traffic conflict. Flown on visual references from outside the cockpit, which is what makes it the contact version, and recovered by 6000 feet AGL.

items.title: Controlled ejection

references.loc: §3.2 — Actual Emergencies and Precautionary Emergency Landings

items.lede: In controlled (planned) ejection the aircrew controls the time and place of the ejection based on fuel state, weather and other factors. There will be time for both aircrew to run the full controlled ejection checklist, coordinate with a chase aircraft if available, and discuss options with the squadron duty officer, RDO and ATC.

items.title: Crew resource management
items.lede: CRM is the use of specifically defined behavioral skills, as an integral part of every flight, to improve mission effectiveness by minimizing crew preventable errors, maximizing crew coordination and optimizing risk management. It covers every crew member, the equipment and the external factors, from before the brief to after the debrief.

items.title: Crosswind computations

references.loc: Part XI Appendix A3 — Crosswind Component

items.lede: The limits are stated as components, but the wind is reported as a direction and a speed. Resolving one into the other is the computation: how much of that wind is across the runway, and how much is down it.

items.title: Crosswind full stops
items.lede: During the landing roll, special attention must be given to maintaining directional control with rudders while maintaining crosswind aileron inputs. While the airplane is decelerating during the landing roll, more and more aileron must be applied to keep the upwind wing from rising. When the airplane is coming to a stop, the aileron control must be held fully towards the winds.

items.title: Crosswind limits
items.lede: The aircraft limit and the training limit are different numbers. NATOPS sets 25 knots of crosswind component on a dry runway; a TW-4 student flying solo gets 10. Know which one is being asked about, because the gap between them is most of the answer.

items.title: Crosswind takeoff and landings
items.lede: The procedures for a takeoff with a crosswind are the same as for a no wind takeoff, except aileron is held into the wind to keep the wings level. Throughout the final, flare and touchdown, the aircraft should track in a straight line down the runway. The application of crosswind correction must be continued as necessary during the landing transition and flare to prevent drift.

items.title: Crosswind touch-and-goes
items.lede: Hold crosswind inputs on the deck and apply upwind aileron to maintain a wings level attitude. Initiate positive, firm, rotation when flying speed is reached to avoid side-slipping.

items.title: Cruise maneuvering
items.lede: Cruise maneuvering will build on the two dimensional fundamentals learned while adding the challenge of maneuvering in the vertical plane as well. During VMC parade turns into and away, Wing was limited to one side or the other from Lead while conducting level turns. Cruise maneuvering will use a fixed power setting, but Wing will now have the ability to change sides as required, using radius of turn principles to maintain the 60° cruise bearing line.

items.title: Day emergency procedures
items.lede: All Navigation routes include a Minimum Safe Altitude for each leg of the planned route and an Emergency Route Abort Altitude for the entire route of flight. A cool head is the pilot's best asset should they become temporarily disoriented. Some situations may dictate an unplanned stop at one of the emergency fields marked on the chart.

items.title: DD-175-1 weather brief
items.lede: The flight weather briefing form. For any flight where part of the intended route is forecast to be IMC, naval aviators shall obtain a flight route weather brief from a DoD-qualified forecaster or an approved forecasting service — so on an instrument cross-country it is not optional.

items.title: DD-1801
items.lede: The DoD international flight plan — the form the flight is filed on. What matters at the brief table is that you filed the route you actually intend to fly, and that you know the civil substitute for the days you are filing from a field that has never seen one.

items.title: Destination maintenance facilities and operating procedures

events.title: Day Navigation
events.label: destination maintenance facilities and operating procedures

references.loc: Ch. 1 §7 — Cross Country and Special Procedures
Appendix A — TW-4 CDO/ODO Aircraft Off-Station Checklist
Appendix B — Squadron CDO/ODO Aircraft Off-Station Checklist
Appendix E — T-6B Dropped Ejection Seat Safety Pin Procedures

items.lede: An off-station aircraft is any aircraft that does not return to KNGP as intended. When an aircraft has a problem off station, the AC notifies their squadron's Command Duty Officer, who in turn notifies the TW-4 CDO. The Wing CDO finalizes the recovery plan with CNATRA DET, who coordinates with the contracted maintenance department.
terms: Destination maintenance facilities and operating procedures

items.title: Direct to a VOR

references.loc: §600 — Direct to a VOR or FMS Waypoint

items.lede: The process used to proceed from your current position direct to a VOR or FMS waypoint. Both versions place the head of the bearing pointer under the heading index on the HSI, then track the new course flying a heading that keeps the CDI centered.

items.title: Discontinued entry
items.lede: Getting out of an OLF entry you should not complete. Five things make it mandatory and immediate, and what you then do depends only on whether you are outside or inside 2 NM Outside 2 NM, turn away from the pattern; inside 2 NM, depart past the upwind numbers.

items.title: Divert to alternate
items.lede: The decision comes before the radio call. Look at the weather at the alternate before you commit — the forecast that qualified it on the ground is hours old by now — and then give ATC a DRAFT report. Changing the flight plan with an FSS instead needs the full format from the IFR Supplement.

items.title: DOR/TTO policy
items.lede: A Training Time Out may be called in any training situation whenever a student or instructor expresses concern for personal safety or a need for clarification of procedures or requirements exists. A Drop on Request is a request to leave flight training.

items.title: Dual concurrence/response CRM

references.loc: §2 — How to Use This Checklist Guide

items.lede: Not every step requires a dual response; however, each pilot, regardless of the seat that they occupy, must ensure each step of the checklist has been accomplished. Items shown as (BOTH) within the checklist indicate dual concurrence is required.

items.title: Eject
items.lede: Ejection handle, pull, both cockpits. There are three ways to think of ejection: immediate, time critical, and controlled (planned). Understanding which of these three scenarios the aircrew is in based on time is essential to making the best decision.

items.title: Ejection seat and CFS
items.lede: The aircraft is equipped with Martin-Baker ejection seats. Each ejection seat is fully automatic, providing safe escape for most combinations of aircraft altitude, speed, attitude and flight path within the aircraft operational envelope. The seat is capable of providing safe escape from zero altitude, zero speed, up to 35,000 feet at speeds up to approximately 370 KIAS.

items.title: Ejection
items.lede: Three kinds, distinguished by how much time you have: immediate, time-critical and controlled. The one that kills people is the controlled ejection that was left too late, so the whole discipline is recognising early which of the three you are in.

items.title: Electrical system malfunctions

numbers.label: Starter in MANUAL drains battery in

items.lede: Generator, generator bus, battery bus, or both batteries. The bus tie is the action that differs: you open it to shed the generator bus and save the battery, and you close it to let a healthy generator carry the battery bus. Getting that backwards is how a single failure becomes a dark cockpit.

items.title: Electrical system
items.lede: A 28 VDC starter/generator as the primary source, a 24 VDC main battery, a small auxiliary battery and an external power receptacle, distributed across a battery bus and a generator bus joined by the bus tie. Almost every electrical question comes down to what the bus tie is doing, because it decides which failures take which equipment.

items.title: Emergency engine shutdown on the ground

events.title: Familiarization Cockpit Procedures
events.label: emergency engine shutdown on the ground

references.loc: Ch. 3 — Emergency Engine Shutdown on the Ground

items.lede: In the event of an engine fire, prop strike or chip light; if the aircraft appears likely to depart the prepared surface; or should any other serious ground emergency occur, accomplish the Emergency Engine Shutdown On The Ground procedure.
terms: Emergency engine shutdown on the ground

items.title: Emergency field selection
items.lede: The first reaction to any emergency encountered in the low level environment is "climb to cope". If the engine fails on a low level, recovery is unlikely unless a suitable landing field is within approximately 3 miles. Chart study for potential emergency diverts before the mission will greatly enhance chances for success.

items.title: Emergency ground egress
items.lede: If emergency egress is required on the ground, perform the procedure after the aircraft has come to a complete stop and the engine has been shut down. In a situation requiring immediate ground egress, the ejection system has the capability for 0/0 ejection.

items.title: Emergency landing pattern
items.lede: A 360-degree pattern that positions the aircraft for landing after a complete power loss, or with an impending failure and enough power left to fly. The keys are high key, low key, base key and final. They are positions over the ground rather than altitudes, and the airspeeds, 120 KIAS minimum to final and 110 KIAS on final, are minimums.

items.title: Emergency orbit pattern
items.lede: The Delta: a racetrack oriented around the duty runway, flown in the same direction as the normal landing pattern, at 2000 feet MSL. It is where you are put when something needs a visual inspection or special assistance, and where everyone goes during a runway change.

items.title: En route descent
items.lede: In the enroute structure, the FAA expects the pilot to descend at an optimum rate consistent with the operating characteristics of the aircraft to 1000 feet above the assigned altitude, and then attempt to descend at a rate of 500 to 1500 FPM until the assigned altitude is reached. Establish and maintain a descent at 200 to 250 KIAS and approximately 4000 FPM.

items.title: En route fuel management
items.lede: The jet log is a prediction, and the flight is the experiment. Compare the estimated times, groundspeeds and fuel flows against what you actually observe, and modify the log as you go. A plan you never check against the gauges is not fuel management.

items.title: En route procedures
items.lede: Due to the increasing complexity of the air traffic system, the terminal phase can be one of the more challenging phases of flight. To maintain constant situational awareness and avoid task saturation, the pilot must know the procedures and stay ahead of the aircraft. To aid in task management, as you approach and enter your terminal area, the mnemonic ABCD can be useful.

items.title: En route weather sources
items.lede: Pilots shall periodically determine that their intended route of flight remains clear of aviation Severe Weather Watch Bulletins and that weather forecasts for each successive intermediate destination and alternate, when required, continue to satisfy the minimums established for the aircraft and the filing status.

items.title: Energy management
items.lede: Energy management is planning a sortie profile that allows maneuvers to be accomplished in an order that optimizes time and energy. Energy level is defined by airspeed, kinetic energy, and altitude, potential energy, and is manipulated with power, drag, and G-loading. Plan maneuvers in an order that minimizes the requirement for deliberate energy changes, and make use of the inherent energy gaining or losing properties of individual maneuvers.

items.title: Engine air starts

numbers.label: Abort if no N1 rise within
Abort if no ITT rise within

items.lede: All airstarts are starter assisted, and which one you fly is decided by the PMU rather than by the engine. PMU NORM is the primary method, being less sensitive to how you move the PCL, and cooler at low airspeed. PMU OFF is for PMU malfunctions only, because you are metering fuel by hand while gliding.

items.title: Engine failure during flight
items.lede: In the event of an engine failure, a decision to eject, land or airstart must be made. The altitude at which the engine fails will determine the time available to perform the procedures.

items.title: Engine failure immediately after takeoff

references.loc: Ch. 3 — Engine Failure Immediately After Takeoff (Sufficient Runway Remaining Straight Ahead)

items.lede: A complete engine failure immediately after takeoff is an extremely critical emergency requiring immediate action and decision making by the pilot. If sufficient runway remains, the best option is to continue straight ahead and land.

items.title: Engine failure indications
items.lede: Loss of power and airspeed; rapid decay in N1, torque and ITT; and the propeller moving towards feather as oil pressure goes. Two gauges are unreliable as to whether the engine has seized, so the indications are read together rather than singly.

items.title: Engine malfunctions
items.lede: Four engine malfunctions and the indications that separate them. Illumination of the fire warning light accompanied by one or more secondary indications is confirmation of an engine fire; a fire warning light with no accompanying indication is not a confirmed fire.

items.title: Engine system
items.lede: The PT6A-68 is a free-turbine turboprop, flat rated at 1100 shaft horsepower as installed. Reverse flow design, in two independent sections: the gas generator at the back makes the gas, and the power section at the front turns it into propeller shaft torque. There is no mechanical connection between the compressor turbine and the power stopped with the gas generator running.

items.title: Exams
items.lede: A check flight is a flight check in any stage of training, and it carries the lesson designator SXX90. All syllabus events have a five- to six-character lesson designator, and the last characters identify the event within the block or the type of event it is.

items.title: FAF-to-MAP timing adjustments
items.lede: The timing FAF to MAP information at the bottom of the aerodrome sketch is used to determine the timing from the FAF to the MAP, at various ground speeds. Where the groundspeed is not one of the tabulated values, the timing must be interpolated.

items.title: Fan break
items.lede: There are two methods of executing the break: interval break or fan break. The fan break is an alternate entry method, initiated with interval by Lead giving the "follow me" signal to Wing. Lead will execute a smooth roll towards 45° AOB at a rate which the Wingman can match. The Wingman will match Lead's roll rate, but will retard the PCL to Idle and extend the speed brake at the beginning of the maneuver to create separation.

items.title: Feeder fixes
items.lede: Feeder fixes put the aircraft on an intercept heading and altitude to be maintained until established on the localizer course. They are one of the transition procedures that establish the aircraft onto the final approach course.

items.title: Feeder routes
items.lede: How you get into a terminal arrival area when the airway does not already take you there. Normally part of a TAA underlies an airway; where it does not, at least one feeder route is provided from an airway fix or NAVAID to the TAA boundary, giving a direct course to the appropriate IF or IAF.

items.title: Feet to rudder placement
items.sourcingLead: Where the feet sit on the rudder pedals — balls of the feet on the pedals, heels on the floor, off the brakes for takeoff and landing. Check the FAM FTI ground procedures and NATOPS Ch. 2 before writing; it is technique taught on the first event rather than a published limit. Pairs with [[seat-height-and-rudder-pedal-adjustment]].

items.title: Fire on ground
items.lede: The primary indications of an engine fire are illumination of the FIRE annunciators. When evidence of a fire exists during start or other ground operations, perform the Emergency Engine Shutdown On The Ground procedure and the Emergency Ground Egress procedure if applicable.

items.title: Fire warning in flight
items.lede: Illumination of the FIRE annunciator indicates the possibility of fire in the engine compartment. Pending confirmation of an engine fire, initiate PEL procedures with the intention of landing as soon as possible.

items.title: Flap failures

references.loc: Ch. 3 — Controllability Check (Structural Damage/Flight Control Malfunction)

items.lede: If uncommanded lateral rolling or yawing is experienced during operation of the wing flaps, an asymmetric flap condition, from a segment binding or the torque link between the inner and outer segments failing. There is enough control authority to counter it at pattern airspeeds, and the procedure is to stop making it worse.

items.title: Flight gear check

references.loc: Ch. IV — FAM21, Familiarization Cockpit Procedures

items.lede: With survival vest on, the student shall locate, identify, and discuss function of each ALSS item.

items.title: Flight Service Station
items.lede: Staffed by FAA-certified pilot weather briefers, an FSS is who you reach at a civil field for weather, NOTAMs, and filing. They are authorised to translate and interpret forecasts and reports for your route — not to create original forecasts, which is the distinction between an FSS brief and a DoD-qualified one.

items.title: Flight split
items.lede: The objective of an in-flight split is to split up a formation so that individual aircraft can safely separate into different working blocks to facilitate single ship high work training. Safe separation can be attained through the use of visual, altitude, lateral, heading, airspeed, or timing differentials. Most commonly, it is best to use a combination of Altitude and Heading separation to achieve a safe flight split.

items.title: FMS arrivals
items.lede: Flying the arrival on the box. The STAR is loaded by name like any other procedure, the FMS transitions itself into terminal phase on the way in, and the handover into the approach is where the work is — because a STAR loaded and an approach loaded do not join themselves.

items.title: FMS flight plan usage

events.title: Radio Instruments
events.label: FMS flight plan usage (SID/STAR, holding, and approach)

items.lede: One rule governs every procedure you put in the box: a published RNAV approach, departure or STAR may not be flown unless it is retrievable by name from a current aircraft navigation database and conforms to the charted procedure. Not assembled by hand out of the same database — retrieved, by name. Everything else here follows from that.
terms: FMS flight plan usage (SID/STAR, holding, and approach)

items.title: FMS procedures
items.lede: The flight management system provides extensive functionality for navigation, flight planning, communications, navigation radio tuning, and simple route and flight plan creation and modification procedures. This functionality is provided using the MFD and UFCP controls. GPS is the highest priority navigation mode of the FMS.

items.title: Forced landing
items.lede: A forced landing is the ELP flown with no engine, after an airstart was not attempted or did not work. With no power available, low energy is corrected by delaying gear and flap extension, intercepting the pattern at a different point, or adjusting the ground track.

items.title: Formation arrival and departure procedures
items.lede: Once safely airborne, Lead levels off to clear the pattern complying with local course rules departure procedures, then sets 80% torque and climbs at 160 KIAS until Wing is in position. The recovery will generally be a VMC recovery via local course rules for the break entry. Approaching the initial VFR entry point, Lead will direct Wing to the Parade Position with enough time to get stabilized prior to the break, then give Wing the appropriate visual signal and conduct the break with clearance from tower.

items.title: Formation communications
items.lede: Your visual or radio communications within the flight must be clear and timely to avoid confusion. The flight will essentially use two call signs: an ATC call sign to communicate with outside agencies and a tactical (TAC) call sign selected by the flight for inter-flight communications. The Formation Lead will conduct all communications with outside controlling agencies, and Wing will monitor and back Lead up as necessary. Lead and Wing must always have direct communication with each other via the pre-briefed tactical frequency, which is confirmed with a positive check-in each time the tactical frequency is changed.

items.title: Formation emergency procedures
items.lede: There are additional considerations when handling emergency situations in formation. As Lead, remember to take into account all actions that will affect the Wing. As Wingman, maintain situational awareness at all times and be ready to assist as requested. In formation, the greatest immediate threat during an emergency is a mid-air collision within the flight. The threat can be alleviated by immediately communicating and taking additional separation, weather permitting, as appropriate.

items.title: Formation maneuvers
items.lede: Parade Position is the basis for all maneuvers in this chapter. It is a fixed position on the left or right 45° bearing from Lead with sufficient wingtip clearance and step-down, utilizing the checkpoints below. Once the flight is established in the area and Ops Checks are complete, the parade sequence begins: a series of tasks which allow both students the opportunity to practice flying basic formation positions and maneuvers.

items.title: Formation position corrections
items.lede: Good formation flying is the result of anticipation and the use of small, timely corrections about all three axes. Strive to maintain perfect positioning, but understand that Wing will only be there for a fleeting moment. What makes a good formation pilot is the ability to recognize and limit deviations and make timely and efficient corrections.

items.title: FTI reference material
items.lede: Each stage of training has an associated Flight Training Instruction containing the information necessary for a student to complete the curriculum satisfactorily, and the SNA is responsible for all material listed in these training instructions. So far as is practical, all information and instructions governing T-6B aircraft procedures and the execution of curriculum maneuvers are published for inclusion in the manual.

items.title: Fuel cutoff gate finger lift guard

events.title: Familiarization Flight 0
events.label: fuel cutoff gate finger lift guard

items.lede: The PCL incorporates a cutoff gate to prevent inadvertent engine shutdown. Where the finger lift guard is fitted, it is pushed down before the PCL cutoff finger lift is raised.
terms: Fuel cutoff gate finger lift guard

items.title: Fuel planning
items.lede: Knowing the fuel state of both aircraft at all times is essential. Lead must know the aircraft with the lowest fuel state in the flight for planning purposes, and the same information is critical if Wing has to assume the Lead. To determine the flight's fuel state, Lead will direct Operations Checks at various points during the flight, then use the lowest fuel state in the flight for planning purposes. Understanding the definitions of Joker, Bingo, and Divert Fuel is required.

items.title: Fuel system

numbers.label: Additional if filled to filler neck

items.lede: 1100 pounds of usable fuel in three integral tanks in a one-piece wing, gravity-fed inboard to a collector tank that feeds the engine. An auto balance system keeps the wings within 20 pounds of each other by shutting off transfer from the light tank, not by moving fuel across.

items.title: Full-stop landings
items.lede: Land smoothly on the main-mounts at the Intended Point of Landing on runway centerline. Landing is divided into three phases: landing transition, flare and touchdown, and landing roll. Each of these phases serves as a transition from the previous phase to the next. The landing roll serves as the transition from landing to taxi, and airspeed is reduced straight-ahead on the runway until at safe taxi speed.

items.title: FWB website and weather brief

events.title: Familiarization Flight 0
events.label: FWB website usage and obtaining weather brief

items.sourcingLead: How the flight weather briefing is obtained and what is required before an event. The FWB site itself and the squadron SOP; the JPPT names the item but does not describe the tool, and the site changes faster than a page could track.
terms: FWB website usage and obtaining weather brief

items.title: GCA pattern
items.lede: In addition to developing basic airwork scan and trim skills, the GCA maneuver incorporates many of the basic skill sets required during execution of a Radar Ground Controlled Approach. In the descent, remember, nose controls airspeed, power controls rate of descent.

items.title: Gear emergencies

references.loc: Ch. 3 — Landing with Unsafe Gear Indications
Ch. 3 — Landing with Cocked Nose Wheel

items.lede: Run the Landing Gear Malfunction checklist any time the gear does not indicate fully up with the handle up or fully down with the handle down. The single most useful thing on the page is the list of safe indications: get any one of them at any point and you stop the checklist and land as soon as practical.

items.title: GPS allowable operations

events.title: Radio Instruments
events.label: GPS allowable operations (GPS waypoints in lieu of NDB, VOR, and TACAN fixes)

items.lede: An FAA approved FMS or GPS system may be used to navigate to, identify, or hold at any waypoints retrieved from an FAA approved and current database. It cannot be used to navigate the final segment, lateral navigation, of any approach that does not have GPS in the title.
terms: GPS allowable operations (GPS waypoints in lieu of NDB, VOR, and TACAN fixes)

items.title: GPS approaches
items.lede: All approaches that contain GPS in the title can be flown using GPS. GPS-equipped aircraft do not need underlying ground-based NAVAIDs or associated aircraft avionics to fly the approach, and monitoring the underlying approach with ground-based NAVAIDs is suggested when able.

items.title: GPS flight modes
items.lede: On entering the terminal area, the FMS transitions to the terminal phase of flight. On leaving the terminal area, the FMS changes from terminal to en-route phase of flight. When a valid GPS approach has been selected and loaded into the active flight plan from the navigation database, the approach phase of flight is activated automatically 2 nm prior to the final approach fix.

items.title: GPS holding
items.lede: An FAA approved FMS or GPS system may be used to hold at any waypoints retrieved from an FAA approved and current database. The entry sectors, the three orbits and the triple drift correction are the same as at any other fix. What differs is how the abeam position is determined and the suffix that shows the FMS has loaded the pattern.

items.title: GPS procedures
items.lede: Area navigation is a method of navigation which permits aircraft operation on any desired flight path within the coverage of ground-based or space-based navigation aids. Pilots are not authorized to fly a published RNAV (GPS) instrument approach procedure, departure procedure, or arrival procedure unless it is retrievable by the procedure name from a current aircraft navigation database and conforms to the charted procedure.

items.title: ATF, ATS, CTS and MIF
items.lede: The standards outlined in Chapter IX, Course Training Standards, are used to evaluate student performance of individual items and maneuvers. The MIF lists the maneuvers a block requires and the proficiency level for each, the ATF records a single event, and the ATS carries the maneuver grades across a training stage.

items.title: Ground handling signals

references.loc: §2 — How to Use This Checklist Guide

items.lede: Communications will be conducted visually whenever practical, provided no sacrifice in operational efficiency is involved. Ground handling signals are shown in NATOPS Figure 8-4-1.

items.title: Ground-speed calculations

references.loc: Appendix B — 60-to-1 Rule and Other Formulas

items.lede: At 60 NM from a NAVAID the distance between each radial is approximately 1 NM. Groundspeed in knots divided by 60 gives NM per minute, which is the form the other en route formulas are built on.

items.title: Half cuban eight
items.lede: This maneuver is a combination of a slightly modified Loop and Immelmann. The maneuver is complete at level flight, with entry airspeed and on reciprocal heading. Select a long, well defined section line which extends behind as well as in front of you.

items.title: Hand signals
items.lede: Your visual or radio communications within the flight must be clear and timely to avoid confusion. The Wingman should have time to acknowledge the signal before Lead executes the maneuver. Execute visual signals high on the canopy, away from the face, in clear view of the Wingman.

items.title: Hard landings
items.lede: Do not raise the gear after a hard landing. Whatever the landing did to the structure, retracting is the one action that can turn a damaged aircraft on the runway into an aircraft that cannot put its gear back down.

items.title: Headwork
items.lede: Headwork and situational awareness is graded on all complete syllabus events. The behavior statement is to maintain situational awareness, and the standard is to demonstrate the ability to minimize the effects of adverse factors and capitalize on opportunities to avoid mission degradation.

items.title: Heavy-weight landing considerations
items.lede: A heavy aircraft needs a faster approach and gives you less time to fix a sink rate. Above 700 to 800 pounds of fuel, expect to fly roughly 3 to 5 knots above the 120/115/110 approach turn airspeeds, and set that up rather than discovering it on the AOA.

items.title: HEFOE
items.lede: HEFOE is a method of signaling system failure when NORDO, using hand signals during the day or a flashlight at night. The use of HEFOE signals assumes that one or both aircraft are NORDO. The signal is preceded by executing a weeping signal, and the aircrew will then indicate which system is affected by passing a corresponding number.

items.title: High altitude approach
items.lede: A high altitude instrument approach enables an aircraft to transition from the high altitude structure to the final approach course for landing. These approaches are routinely executed by high performance military aircraft into military aerodromes to maintain efficient fuel consumption, higher TAS, and to avoid low altitude weather until closer to the destination.

items.title: HILO approach
items.lede: The Holding Pattern Approach, or Holding In Lieu Of procedure turn, is a type of procedure turn. The HILO approach uses a published holding pattern to reverse course and establish the aircraft inbound on the intermediate or final approach course. HILO approaches are printed using a normal holding pattern track with a heavy line indicating in lieu of procedure turn. Unlike the teardrop and procedure turn approaches, the holding pattern approach will always have a FAF depicted on the approach.

items.title: Holding corrections
items.lede: Compensate for wind effects by flying drift corrected headings on the inbound and outbound legs while making appropriate timing adjustments. Adjust outbound heading and time to compensate for wind so that the turn inbound will place the aircraft on the holding course and, where leg lengths are established by timing, with an appropriate amount of inbound time.

items.title: Holding entry
items.lede: Upon arrival at the holding fix, the entry turn will be made towards the general direction given in the holding clearance. The specific heading needed to establish the aircraft in the designated holding airspace is determined by the type of holding pattern being used, standard pattern or non-standard pattern, and by comparing aircraft heading with the reciprocal of the holding course. There are three basic types of entry turns: parallel, teardrop and direct.

items.title: Holding
items.lede: Holding is a predetermined maneuver that keeps aircraft within a specified airspace until further clearance is received from ATC. It can be accomplished at an intersection, GPS waypoint, radial/DME fix, or at a navigation facility. When ATC clears you to hold, a specified airspace oriented around the holding fix has been reserved, clear of other traffic. The extent of the cleared airspace is based on maximum holding airspeed as listed in the FLIP GP and FAA AIM.

items.title: Home field arrival
items.lede: Every KNGP arrival funnels to one place. Whichever route you come in on, you are flying it at 240 KIAS to Point SHAMROCK, and from SHAMROCK the arrival is the same for everyone: slow to 200, call tower, and take the overhead or the straight-in.

items.title: Hot start

numbers.label: Abort if ITT likely to exceed
Abort if ITT likely to remain

items.lede: In the AUTO start mode, if a hot start is projected the PMU should terminate the start sequence. The engine start should be aborted manually if the ITT rate of increase appears likely to exceed 1000 °C, or if ITT appears likely to remain between 871 and 1000 °C for more than 5 seconds.

items.title: HSI orientation
items.lede: For overall orientation, consider the VOR station always located at the center of the HSI card and the aircraft's position on the tail of the bearing pointer. The VOR provides 360 magnetic courses called radials, which radiate from the station like spokes from the hub of a wheel. Unless the bearing pointer is on the heading index, as the aircraft moves forward, heads will fall and tails will rise.

items.title: HUD
items.lede: The HUD in the forward cockpit and the HUD repeater on the right MFD provide display of aircraft flight, navigation and tactical data; simulated weapon inventory and status indication; ARM/SAFE/SIM condition; a fixed steering cue for manual weapon employment; and air-to-air and air-to-ground weapon employment solutions and steering commands.

items.title: Hung start

numbers.label: Auto-abort if N1 acceleration to idle

items.lede: In the AUTO start mode, if a hung start is projected the PMU should terminate the start sequence. The engine start should be aborted manually if normal N1 increase is halted.

items.title: Hydraulic system malfunctions
items.lede: Normal operation of landing gear, flaps, speed brake and nosewheel steering should be considered unavailable when the HYD FL LO caution is illuminated and pressure is below 1800 psi, or when hydraulic pressure is rapidly decreasing toward or reads 0 psi. When the EHYD PX LO caution is illuminated, the emergency landing gear and flap extension system should be considered inoperative.

items.title: Hydraulic system
items.lede: One engine-driven pump, about five quarts, powering the landing gear and inboard main gear doors, the flaps, the speed brake and nose wheel steering. An emergency accumulator charged by the normal system gives one shot at extending the gear and flaps if the normal system is gone. It is a single actuation, because the pump cannot recharge it once it has been released.

items.title: Hyperventilation and hypoxia
items.lede: Hypoxia is a general term that describes a state of oxygen deficiency in the tissues. Hypocapnia is low CO2 in the blood resulting from hyperventilation. Adverse physiological conditions have common symptoms similar to other adverse physiological conditions, making it difficult to discern the root cause of physiological symptoms during flight.

items.title: IAC failure
items.lede: Dual IAC failure will result in the loss of HUD, UFCP and MFD displays in both cockpits. Loss of a single IAC may not cause an IAC1 FAIL or IAC2 FAIL message to be displayed, but may cause loss of MFD displays in one or both cockpits, erratic MFD displays, or IAC synchronization errors. The HUD and UFCP may, or may not, be operating properly.

items.title: Icing
items.lede: The aircraft has been approved only for transit through light rime icing conditions. Prolonged flight in known icing conditions is prohibited and must be avoided. The aircraft includes protection for critical systems and cockpit displays through the use of heated pitot masts and a heated angle-of-attack sensor.

items.title: IFR clearance from uncontrolled airports

events.title: Radio Instruments
events.label: obtaining IFR clearance from uncontrolled airports

items.lede: Where there is no clearance delivery, an IFR clearance may be obtained in one of several ways. Which are available is a property of the field, listed in the IFR Supplement and posted on signs around the airport. A clearance obtained on the ground by telephone carries a void time, and you must depart before it.
terms: obtaining IFR clearance from uncontrolled airports

items.title: IFR flight planning

events.title: Instrument Check Flight
events.label: flight planning (submit a completed DD-1801 and jet log: Stopover flight plan to include an en route holding delay (1st leg), and terminal delay (2nd leg))

references.loc: §4.5.5 — Stopover Flights Within the Contiguous United States

items.lede: Before flight the pilot in command shall be familiar with all available information appropriate to the intended operation. That is the whole requirement, and everything else on the page is what "all available information" turns out to mean on a cross-country to a field you have never seen.
terms: flight planning (submit a completed DD-1801 and jet log: Stopover flight plan to include an en route holding delay (1st leg), and terminal delay (2nd leg))

items.title: IFR pick-up
items.lede: The IFR flight plan is filed on the ground from the working block to the desired destination, the local area or the valley, and a local letter of agreement allows the clearance to be picked up in the air. Until a change of flight plan is filed and an IFR clearance obtained, the flight remains in VFR conditions.

items.title: IFR Supplement
items.lede: The airport and facility directory for IFR operations. Three sections plus the covers, and the covers are the part students forget: the inside back cover carries the FAA formats for position reports, changing a flight plan and filing in flight, and the outside back cover carries the ICAO versions.

items.title: IFR to VFR transition

references.loc: Appendix D — CTW-4 Closed Tower Operating Procedures

items.lede: It is the responsibility of the pilot in command to ensure that the proper agency is notified of flight termination. Cancellation of an instrument flight plan does not meet the requirement for closing out the flight plan; when a landing report has been properly delivered, the flight plan will be considered closed out.

items.title: IFR unusual attitudes
items.lede: Recognize and recover from an unusual attitude with reference to instruments only. An unusual attitude is any unexpected or inadvertent attitude encountered during normal instrument flight. Use the attitude indicator as the main recovery instrument after its proper operation is verified and an unusual attitude is confirmed. The recovery is complete when the desired attitude for normal instrument flight is attained.

items.title: ILS approach
items.lede: The Instrument Landing System is a precision approach system that provides azimuth and glideslope information to the pilot. It consists of a highly directional localizer and glideslope transmitter with associated marker beacons, compass locators, and at some sites, Distance Measuring Equipment. The system is automatically monitored and provides changeover to a standby localizer or glideslope transmitter when the main system malfunctions. Because both course and glidepath information is provided, it constitutes a precision approach and DA/DH minimums may be used.

items.title: ILS full procedure turn
items.lede: A procedure turn flown onto an ILS. D LIDS is set up after the IAF, and the outbound leg is flown on the front course rather than on a separate published outbound course. The front course stays set in the CDI throughout.

items.title: IMC emergencies
items.lede: The flight manual provides the best possible operating instructions under most circumstances, but it is not a substitute for sound judgement. Multiple emergencies, adverse weather, terrain, etc. may require modification of the procedures.

items.title: IMC lost communications

references.loc: Briefing Guide — Lost Comms NGP Departure

items.lede: The local area lost communications procedures are published in the KNGP In-Flight Guide rather than the FIH. Which of the four cases applies depends on how far along the departure or recovery the failure occurs: after takeoff, on a local coded flight plan, in the GCA pattern, or on GCA final. All four end by proceeding direct to an approach aid or fix serving NAS Corpus Christi and executing a published approach to the runway in use.

items.title: Immediate air-start

numbers.label: Discontinue if no N1 rise in
Abort if no ITT rise in

items.lede: The Immediate Airstart (PMU NORM) procedure should be used following engine failure at low altitude when thrust requirements are critical, or when time and conditions do not permit completing a full airstart procedure.

items.title: Immelmann
items.lede: The Immelmann is a half Loop followed by a half roll, all flown in the same vertical plane. The maneuver is complete after a momentary pause in level flight with wings level on an opposite heading from entry. This maneuver offers a quick means of reversing the direction of flight while trading excess airspeed for increased altitude.

items.title: Impending engine failure indications
items.lede: The indications that the engine is failing while it is still running. Any of them is grounds for a PEL. The longer the engine runs, the greater the chance of complete failure.

items.title: I'M SAFE checklist
items.lede: I'M SAFE is the personal preflight: six questions asked of yourself before the brief, not before the walk. Proper aircrew coordination begins with the individual crew member, and situational awareness can already be degraded before you set foot in the cockpit.

items.title: Inadvertent instrument flight
items.lede: If a formation flight inadvertently enters IMC conditions, Lead will transition to an instrument scan. Wing will maintain Parade Position and continue their scan on Lead. Lead should determine the best way to exit IMC. If unable to return to VMC, ensure proper terrain clearance and contact ATC to pick up an IFR clearance for the flight, or separate clearances for each individual aircraft.

items.title: Inadvertent thunderstorm penetration
items.lede: Flights through thunderstorms or other areas of extreme turbulence should be avoided due to the possibility of engine flameout, structural failure, or damage due to hail, lightning, and violent up and down drafts. Should flight through an area of thunderstorm activity become unavoidable, the following procedures should be used.

items.title: Inadvertent trim actuation
items.lede: Trim moved when you did not mean to move it, or kept moving after you let go. The first action is to take the trim system out of the loop with the interrupt button; the second is to use airspeed to make the stick forces manageable while you work out what happened.

items.title: Incipient spin recovery
items.lede: Incipient spins are the spin-like motion that occurs between a post-stall gyration and a fully developed spin. The incipient spin phase lasts approximately two turns. In order to recover from the incipient spin, execute the INADVERTENT DEPARTURE FROM CONTROLLED FLIGHT Procedure.

items.title: Instrument scan patterns
items.lede: The concept of attitude flying is based upon the fact that a specific power setting when combined with a specific attitude will result in a specific aircraft performance. Once PAT is accomplished, scan to maintain the desired performance. Scan is the systematic process of monitoring the crosscheck and performance instruments to detect deviation from desired flight parameters, then applying the proper controls to make an appropriate timely correction. The goal is early error detection and correction.

items.title: Integrated (VMC) scan
items.lede: In introducing the basic flight maneuvers, the integrated flight instruction method will be used. This means that each flight maneuver will be performed by using both outside visual references and the flight instruments. The task of scanning in contact flying involves division of attention between the external and internal environment, setting attitudes with the nose and wings in relation to the horizon, and cross-checking them against the instruments in the cockpit.

items.title: Intentional spin entry
items.lede: Two primary factors must be present for an aircraft to spin: stalled AOA and yaw, rotation about the vertical axis. The spin entry is straightforward and procedural; the spin entry is not a finesse maneuver. It requires full back stick with ailerons neutral, fully deflected rudder, and PCL to idle. Practice spins to the left and right.

items.title: Intersections
items.lede: An intersection is a navigational fix that can be defined in the T-6B using VOR/DME, VOR only, the intersection of two or more radials from two or more NAVAIDs, or GPS. Intersections are used to identify significant points along departure procedures, airways, arrivals, holding areas, approach procedures, and missed approaches. When referencing two or more NAVAIDs, the primary NAVAID is the one used to navigate a track to the intersection, and a secondary NAVAID is one that provides a crosscut to identify the intersection along the primary track.

items.title: Inverted spin

references.loc: Ch. 3 — Inadvertent Departure from Controlled Flight

items.lede: Inverted spins are prohibited, so this is a recognition item. It is entered by releasing the controls at high nose attitude and low airspeed with power on: the aircraft torque rolls left to a near-inverted, nose-level attitude and departs. It is flatter than an erect spin and the recovery differs in one control.

items.title: Jet log
items.lede: A completed jet log is required for every event whose syllabus notes call for one, with a copy for the instructor. It is a prediction of times, groundspeeds and fuel, and its purpose is to be compared against reality in flight — a log filled in on the ground and never looked at again has done nothing.

items.title: Knock-it-off
items.lede: Knock-it-off is a radio call used by a flight member to alert the formation to cease maneuvering. It is used when safety of flight is an issue, such as an emergency, a traffic threat, or a crewmember who has G-locked due to poor Anti-G Straining Maneuver execution during Tail Chase. This radio call should be preserved as an "unexpected stop and attention getter" and may be initiated by any flight member.

items.title: Landing flap landings
items.lede: The approach is a descending 180° balanced turn to final in the flaps Up, TO, or LDG configuration. In the landing flap configuration, add power as required to maintain 120 KIAS on Downwind, approximately 52% torque, and at the 180 lower the nose to the 110 KIAS approach attitude.

items.title: Landing gear emergency extension
items.lede: Do not use the Landing Gear Emergency Extension checklist unless directed by the Landing Gear Malfunction, Hydraulic System Malfunctions, Battery Bus Inoperative, or the Battery and Generator Failure checklists.

items.title: Landing gear inspection

references.loc: §3.2 — Actual Emergencies and Precautionary Emergency Landings

items.lede: The aircraft with an unsafe gear indication should climb to an emergency orbit or delta pattern in accordance with local SOP or Course Rules, and coordinate with the Wingman to get an airborne landing gear inspection. The inspection should be conducted at a minimum of 2000 feet AGL. At no time shall student solos join-up to inspect landing gear.

items.title: Landing irregularities
items.lede: A deviation from a normal landing which could cause a dangerous situation to quickly develop. Airspeed in the flare is only slightly above stall airspeed, and even at slow airspeeds the elevator is still very effective, so an abrupt change in pitch could result in a balloon, a bounce, or even a stall.

items.title: Landing pattern stalls

events.title: Familiarization
events.label: landing pattern (approach turn and landing attitude) stalls

items.lede: Proper recognition of and recovery from approach-to-stall conditions in the landing pattern. Training emphasis is on recognition of approach-to-stall indications and appropriate recovery procedures. Recover at first indication of stall, airframe buffet or stick shaker, whichever occurs first. Do not enter a full stall.
terms: landing pattern (approach turn and landing attitude) stalls

items.title: Landing pattern
items.lede: The landing pattern is a geometric racetrack-shaped course flown so that an approach and landing may be executed in a systematic sequence. The landing line, the upwind leg, and the parallel Downwind leg form the sides of the racetrack pattern. These lines are joined together by the Crosswind turn and by the approach turn at the Downwind end of the pattern. The landing pattern is subdivided into three parts: the pattern, approach, and landing.

items.title: Lead, lag and pure pursuit

events.title: Formation
events.label: principles of lead, lag and pure pursuit

items.lede: The concept of pursuit geometry between aircraft is fundamental to formation maneuvering. This geometry relates specifically to flight paths and planes of motion. Assuming both aircraft are moving forward at the same speed and in the same plane of motion, aircraft nose position relative to the other aircraft will determine the type of pursuit. There are three basic types of pursuit: lead, pure and lag.
terms: principles of lead, lag and pure pursuit

items.title: Level speed change
items.lede: Level Speed Changes are taught to familiarize you with the various trim adjustments required with changes in airspeed, power setting, and aircraft configuration. The sequence is flown from normal cruise, 200 KIAS, to the no flap configuration, 120 KIAS, to the landing flap configuration, 120 KIAS, and then to normal cruise, 200 KIAS.

items.title: Local area departure
items.lede: Inform Navy Corpus Ground of departure intentions when calling for taxi. On a beach-line departure, climb to 500 feet MSL at 200 KIAS on the heading published for the runway in use, then turn heading 105 toward the beach line and climb to 2500 feet MSL.

items.title: Local area flight procedures
items.sourcingLead: TW-4 SOP Ch. 1 for the wing-wide provisions and Ch. 2 for the T-6B chapter — not Ch. 3 or Ch. 4, which are other type chapters. Then Course Rules Manual Ch. 2 §3, Primary Working Areas, p. 2-15, for area boundaries, altitudes, entry and departure, and the area working frequencies. The squadron SOPs (VT-27, VT-28) are the layer below that and are scans with no extractable text, so anything from them has to be read off a rendered page. Keep the page to what a student says at the table: what the areas are, how you get in and out of one, what you may and may not do inside it, and the fuel and weather gates. Leave the departure and arrival routings alone — those are the Course Rules tab's, and this page should not restate them.

items.title: Local cross-country SOP

references.loc: Ch. 1 §7 — Cross Country and Special Procedures

items.lede: A cross-country flight is defined as a flight operating outside the local flying area or remaining overnight at an enroute destination airfield outside the Corpus Christi local area. The TW-4 SOP sets the local flying area, the wing request deadline, check-in, aircraft security and contract fuel, and each squadron SOP sets its own request deadline.

items.title: Local night VNAV SOP
items.lede: Nighttime Visual Navigation routes shall not be flown lower than 2000 feet AGL. Aircraft must not operate within a SIGMET at night unless they have an operable radar installed capable of detection and avoidance of isolated thunderstorms. Aerobatics, short breaks, formation and stalls are prohibited at night.

items.title: Local VFR sectional review
items.lede: The sectional is a schematic: a simplified, generalized, codified selection of features, annotated with names, numbers and boundaries.

items.title: Localizer approach
items.lede: A non-precision approach flown on the localizer component of an ILS. The course guidance and the way you get established are identical to the ILS; the procedures and the minimums are non-precision. So you fly it with 6 Ts at the FAF, level at an MDA, and go to a MAP rather than a decision altitude.

items.title: Loop
items.lede: The Loop is a 360° turn in the vertical plane with constant heading and nose track. Because it is executed in a single plane, the elevator is the principal control surface. Ailerons and rudder are used to maintain directional control and coordinated flight. The maneuver is complete when wings are level at the horizon on the same heading as at entry.

items.title: Loss of START READY light during start sequence

events.title: Familiarization Cockpit Procedures
events.label: loss of start ready light during start sequence

items.lede: The engine start should be aborted manually if the PCL is moved or the ST READY green advisory message extinguishes during the start sequence. If the ST READY advisory extinguishes for any reason during the start sequence, the PMU will no longer provide automatic protection.
terms: Loss of START READY light during start sequence

items.title: Lost aircraft procedures
items.lede: Admit it early and use the radios, the navaids, the FMS nearest function. The failure mode is not being lost, it is flying around lost until the fuel runs out, so the aim is to be on deck somewhere suitable rather than found.

items.title: Lost communication procedures
items.lede: Radio failure in a formation is a potentially confusing and hazardous situation. If NORDO, all radios have failed. The formation should maintain VMC if able. The lead position should be offered to the NORDO aircraft in order to troubleshoot and attempt to re-establish radio communications. If radio contact cannot be re-established, the aircraft with the good radios shall take the Lead position to return to base.

items.title: Lost communications
items.lede: During two-way radio communications failure, when confronted with a situation not covered in the regulation, pilots are expected to exercise good judgment in whatever action they elect to take. The transponder should be adjusted to reply on Mode 3/A, Code 7600, and pilots can expect ATC to attempt to communicate by transmitting on guard frequencies and available frequencies of navaids. If able to maintain flight in VMC, continue flight under VFR and land as soon as practicable and notify ATC.

items.title: Lost sight procedures
items.lede: Lost sight is the term used by the Wingman to communicate that they have lost visual contact with the Lead aircraft during IMC conditions. During IMC formation flight, Wing will have very little reference to attitude, as their scan should be nearly solely on Lead's aircraft. If Wing loses sight of Lead, it may take Wing several seconds to transition to an effective instrument scan and transmit the "lost sight" radio call. For this reason, a smooth reduction of power once lost sight conditions are recognized is essential to reduce the likelihood of a mid-air.

items.title: Low fuel pressure
items.lede: If engine fuel feed pressure drops below 10 psi, and the boost pump fails to engage automatically, the FUEL PX warning will illuminate. If engine fuel feed pressure is fluctuating at or below 10 psi, the boost pump will alternately cycle on and off, illuminating and extinguishing the BOOST PUMP advisory.

items.title: Maneuvering speed
items.lede: VO is 227 KIAS: the speed above which full or abrupt control movement in one axis can cause structural damage. Below it the wing stalls before the airframe is overloaded; above it, it does not.

items.title: Maneuvering speeds

numbers.label: Upright flight between negative G sets

references.loc: Ch. 5 — Turbulent Air Penetration Speed Limitations (VG)

items.lede: Operating maneuvering speed (VO) is the speed above which full or abrupt control movements in one axis can result in structural damage to the aircraft. VO is 227 KIAS. Full rudder deflection above 150 KIAS, however, will exceed the limits for the rudder control system.

items.title: Memorized checklists

references.loc: §2 — How to Use This Checklist Guide

items.lede: Most checklists are not performed from memory; however, the following checklists performed during critical phases of flight must be performed from memory: Lineup, After Takeoff, Operations, and Before Landing.

items.title: Minimum fuel requirements

numbers.label: Solo, depart KNGT or K4 MOA

items.lede: Aircraft shall carry fuel to fly from takeoff to the destination airfield, plus a reserve of 10 percent of the planned fuel requirement. In no case shall the planned fuel reserve after the final landing be less than 20 minutes of flight.

items.title: Missed approach
items.lede: A missed approach is a procedure used to discontinue an instrument approach if the runway environment is not in sight, or the aircraft is not in a position to make a safe landing. The primary concern if unable to land is to climb to a safe altitude. Therefore, establishing and maintaining a positive rate of climb should be your first priority if a missed approach is commenced. Your second priority should be to turn the aircraft, if required, to intercept the missed approach course or to the designated heading.

items.title: NATOPS limitations
items.lede: Chapter 5. The airspeeds and the G limits are what get asked cold; the engine table is what you are actually watching in flight. Two habits are worth more than memorising the lot: know which limits change with configuration, and know which ones the PMU is holding for you and therefore what an exceedance means about the system.

items.title: Night cockpit setup
items.lede: All instruments, control panels, and displays in both cockpits are lighted for operation during night or reduced light conditions. The NIGHT position is intended for use during night and low light operation, and if NIGHT mode is selected in either cockpit, the MFDs and UFCPs in the whole aircraft are placed into the night mode.

items.title: Night emergency procedures
items.lede: Comply with the NATOPS Flight Manual. If the engine fails at or above 2000 feet AGL, a restart is not attempted or unsuccessful, and a lighted runway is not immediately available, ejection is highly recommended. If the engine fails below 2000 feet AGL, attempting a restart is not recommended.

items.title: Night flying considerations
items.lede: Night takes away the cues you have been flying on and replaces them with fewer, ambiguous ones. Protect your dark adaptation, stop trusting your sense of distance, and expect the instruments to be doing more of the work than they did in daylight.

items.title: Night VFR chart interpretation
items.lede: Obstructions are marked and lighted to warn pilots of their presence during daytime and nighttime conditions. Most have aviation red obstruction lights, and obstructions with high intensity flashing white lights are depicted with an obstruction symbol with lightning bolts coming from the top. When planning night Visual Navigation Routes, consideration should be given to using thicker and darker lines for routes, with larger print for all associated magnetic courses, fuel, and timing requirements.

items.title: Night VNAV timing and course corrections

events.title: Night Navigation
events.label: night VNAV timing and course corrections

items.lede: Nighttime Visual Navigation routes shall not be flown lower than 2000 feet AGL. In uncontrolled airspace, the night cloud clearance and visibility requirements are 3 SM with 500 feet below, 1000 feet above and 2000 feet horizontal from clouds.
terms: Night VNAV timing and course corrections

items.title: No-flap landings
items.lede: The approach is a descending 180° balanced turn to final in the flaps Up, TO, or LDG configuration. In the no flap configuration, add power as required to maintain 120 KIAS on Downwind, approximately 31% torque, and at the 180 lower the nose to the 120 KIAS approach attitude. A flap-up landing will not require a transition until the 180.

items.title: No-gyro approach
