items.lede: A no-gyro approach is available to a pilot under radar control who experiences circumstances wherein the directional gyro or other stabilized compass is inoperative or inaccurate. When this occurs, the pilot should so advise ATC and request a no-gyro vector or approach.

items.title: No start
items.lede: In the AUTO start mode, if a no start is detected the PMU should terminate the start sequence. The engine start should be aborted manually if no rise of ITT is evident within 10 seconds after fuel flow indications.

items.title: No-wind orbit
items.lede: The second passage of the holding fix commences the no-wind orbit. A no-wind orbit is used to determine the general wind direction and any heading and timing adjustments that will be needed to offset their effects.

items.title: Non-radar environment communications

references.loc: §C117 — Additional Mandatory Reports for Non-Radar Environment

items.lede: Federal Aviation Regulations require pilots to maintain a listening watch on the appropriate frequency and to furnish position reports passing certain reporting points. Reporting points are indicated by symbol on enroute charts: the designated compulsory reporting point symbol is the solid triangle and the on request reporting point symbol is an open triangle. Reports passing an on request reporting point are only necessary when requested by ATC.

items.title: Normal takeoff
items.lede: Takeoff is the movement of the aircraft from its starting point on the runway until it leaves the ground in controlled flight. Although a relatively simple maneuver, the takeoff presents numerous potential hazards: the dynamics of high engine thrust, possible directional control problems, the potential for runway incursions, high-speed aborts and low-altitude engine failures make the takeoff regime of flight unique in its safety challenges. Although the takeoff and climb process is one continuous maneuver, it is divided into three separate steps for purposes of explanation: takeoff roll, rotation, and initial climb.

items.title: NOTAMs

events.title: Radio Instruments
events.label: NOTAM to include local, FDC, center, special notices, International/Domestic Notices, and GPS

items.lede: A NOTAM is a notice containing information concerning the establishment, condition, or change in any component, facility, service, procedure, or hazard in the National Airspace System, the timely knowledge of which is essential to personnel concerned with flight operations. NOTAM information is not known far enough in advance to be publicized by other means.
terms: NOTAM to include local, FDC, center, special notices, International/Domestic Notices, and GPS

items.title: OBOGS and pressurization system
items.lede: Both run on conditioned engine bleed air, which is why an engine failure or a total electrical failure takes the oxygen and the cockpit pressure together. OBOGS makes oxygen continuously from bleed air, so there is no duration limit and no bottle to watch. What the system provides instead is a plenum, two anti-suffocation valves and the seat bottle, in that order of use.

items.title: OBOGS FAIL message
items.lede: Illumination of the OBOGS FAIL message is a positive indication of a system malfunction. Failure of the OBOGS system may be accompanied by reduced pressure or quantity of breathing gas and may result in hypoxia symptoms if corrective action is not taken immediately.

items.title: OBOGS malfunctions
items.lede: Illumination of the OBOGS FAIL message is a positive indication of a system malfunction. OBOGS system failure may also occur without either message illumination and may be indicated by physiological symptoms. If physiological symptoms are recognized at any point, proceed immediately to the OBOGS Failure/Overtemp/Physiological Symptoms checklist.

items.title: Obstacle departure procedures
items.lede: Obstacle departure procedures provide obstruction clearance from the terminal area to the appropriate enroute structure. Found in DOD FLIP approach plates, ODPs will be labeled with the word OBSTACLE in the title.

items.title: Oil and propeller systems
items.lede: The propeller is an oil-driven system. Pressurised engine oil pushes the pitch change piston forward toward fine, and when that pressure is reduced the counterweights and the feathering spring drive the blades coarse. That is why an engine failure sends the propeller toward feather on its own, and why every oil indication is also a propeller indication.

items.title: Oil system malfunction or low oil pressure

events.title: Familiarization Emergency Procedures Trainer
events.label: oil system malfunction or low oil pressure

numbers.label: Check OIL TRX CB if pressure

references.loc: Ch. 3 — Oil System Malfunction or Low Oil Pressure

items.lede: Use this procedure for any of the following: red OIL PX annunciator illuminated, amber OIL PX annunciator illuminated, oil pressure fluctuations, oil temperature out of limits, or visibly confirmed leaking oil from the aircraft.
terms: Oil system malfunction or low oil pressure

items.title: OLF arrival and departure
items.lede: The outlying field entry is a series of uniform procedures by which aircraft enter the landing pattern. Since numerous aircraft may be using the same outlying field simultaneously, it is absolutely necessary that each aircraft conform to the same systematic pattern and standard operating procedures for safety and efficiency. Goliad is the primary OLF for TW-4 T-6 aircraft.

items.title: OLF course rules

events.title: RDO Pattern Party
events.label: OLF Course rules for field of use

events.title: RDO Pattern Party
events.label: OLF Course rules for field of use

items.lede: The rules that govern the outlying field itself, as opposed to the procedure for entering it: whether the field is open, how many aircraft it will hold, where wave-offs and practice PELs go, and how the pattern is reconfigured when the runway changes. Goliad is the primary OLF for TW-4 T-6 aircraft.
terms: OLF Course rules for field of use

items.title: OLF/RDO communication
items.lede: The RDO does not clear anyone to land. Every call at an OLF is advisory, sequencing is a conversation, and responsibility for interval stays with the aircraft flying it. What the RDO gives you is the runway, the count, and the word to go around if the pattern cannot take you.

items.title: Out-of-control flight

events.title: Familiarization
events.label: OCF recovery and airborne damaged aircraft

references.loc: Ch. 3 — Inadvertent Departure from Controlled Flight

items.lede: A situation in which the aircraft does not respond immediately and in a normal sense to application of flight controls is considered out-of-control flight or a departure. OCF is the seemingly random motion of the aircraft about one or more axes, usually resulting from a stalled condition in which the inertial forces on the aircraft exceed the authority of the aerodynamic controls. In general, OCF can be divided into three categories: poststall gyrations, incipient spins, and steady-state spins.
terms: OCF recovery and airborne damaged aircraft

items.title: Over-the-station intercepts

numbers.label: Turn to intercept if course change over

items.lede: An over-the-station intercept is a procedure used to intercept and fly outbound on a specific radial immediately after station passage. This procedure is appropriate during airways navigation and instrument approaches that use VOR facilities for enroute navigation, initial approach fixes, final approach fixes or missed approach procedures. Upon station passage, perform the 6 Ts as appropriate.

items.title: PAR approach
items.lede: During a PAR approach, the controller utilizes an airport surveillance radar system to transition the aircraft to final and then hands off to another controller. This final controller utilizes a precision radar system located at the airport to provide precise course, range and glideslope feedback during the final approach segment. Because both course and glideslope information is available, it constitutes a precision approach.

items.title: PAR without glideslope

references.loc: §907 — Airport Surveillance Approach (ASR) and PAR Without Glideslope (PAR W/O GS)

items.lede: Because glideslope information is either not available or not used, the ASR and PAR W/O GS approaches are both non-precision, and both are accomplished using the same procedures. The PAR W/O GS uses the ASR to establish the aircraft on final and then hands the aircraft off to a final controller who utilizes only the azimuth portion of the precision radar to provide course and range information. Due to the increased accuracy of course and range information available during the PAR W/O GS, the associated MDA may be lower.

items.title: Pattern adjustments for crosswinds
items.lede: Compensate for crosswinds in the landing pattern to maintain the normal ground track. All pilots should be able to assess crosswinds and understand how they affect pattern operations. The proper application of crosswind controls is essential to executing landings.

items.title: PCL cutoff and inadvertent engine shutdown

events.title: Familiarization Flight 0
events.label: PCL cutoff and inadvertent engine shutdown

items.lede: The PCL incorporates a cutoff gate to prevent inadvertent engine shutdown. Mishaps have occurred due to inadvertent lifting of the PCL idle cutoff gate during flight, and an engine shutting down after an inadvertent movement to cutoff is not relit by moving the PCL back to idle.
terms: PCL cutoff and inadvertent engine shutdown

items.title: PEL from the pattern

references.loc: §705 — Precautionary Emergency Landing from the Pattern

items.lede: The same PEL, entered from the landing pattern rather than from the working area. The indications of impending engine failure are the same ones; what changes is that you are already low, already slow and already surrounded by traffic, so the ELP is intercepted at or before low key instead of at high key.

items.title: PMU NORM air-start

numbers.label: Discontinue if no N1 rise in
Abort if no ITT rise in

items.lede: The PMU NORM airstart procedure will provide the least complicated airstart. It is considered the primary method since it is less sensitive to the rate of PCL movement, and cooler starts can be expected at lower airspeeds. Refer to the PMU OFF airstart if the PMU FAIL message is present.

items.title: PMU OFF air-start

numbers.label: Discontinue if no N1 rise in
Abort if no ITT rise in

items.lede: If the PMU has malfunctioned, with the PMU FAIL warning illuminated, conduct the airstart with the PMU off. With the PMU off, the igniters will not automatically activate and must be selected manually.

items.title: Point-to-point
items.lede: If a NAVAID transmits both radial and DME information and the aircraft equipment is capable of processing that information, it can be used to navigate from present position to a specific radial and DME from that station via the most direct path. If cleared direct to a radial/DME fix, the pilot may be radar vectored or employ point to point navigation. For PTP navigation, the turn to an initial heading should be initiated as soon as possible once cleared.

items.title: Power-off stall
items.lede: Stall the aircraft in a power-off condition to demonstrate the proper recovery when no power is available. Power-off stalls are flown to practice recovery from potentially dangerous low airspeed conditions prior to high key and during the ELP. Airspeed may decrease for various reasons, including inattention, task saturation, and attempts to stretch the glide to regain profile.

items.title: Power-on stalls
items.lede: Stall the aircraft in a power-on condition to demonstrate the proper recovery when power is available. Aircraft pitch and bank angle will be held constant until un-commanded nose drop and/or unplanned rolling motion. An entry speed of 150 KIAS results in about 1500 to 2000 feet altitude gain.

items.title: Precautionary emergency landing

numbers.label: PCL to OFF if unable to hold

references.loc: Ch. 2 §4 — Flights Following PEL or Emergency Landing
§3.2 — Actual Emergencies and Precautionary Emergency Landings

items.lede: The PEL procedure should be executed whenever indications of a possible engine failure exist or when directed by the checklist. Use power, airspeed, altitude and configuration to intercept and maintain the emergency landing pattern profile.

items.title: Any previously discussed familiarization items
items.lede: The Familiarization maneuvers already briefed, any of which can be asked. The list below is generated from the syllabus rather than written out, so it stays in step with the events themselves.

items.title: Any previously discussed item
items.lede: The check flight can reach back to anything. Not just the maneuvers — every discuss item the stage has briefed, from the airwork in the UTD to the flight planning on the last cross-country. The list below is built from the syllabus rather than written out, so it stays in step with the events themselves.

items.title: Any previously discussed maneuver

events.title: Day Familiarization
events.label: any previously discussed maneuver or procedure

items.lede: The maneuvers already briefed, any of which you can be asked about. The list below is built from the syllabus rather than written out, so it stays in step with the events themselves.
terms: any previously discussed maneuver or procedure

items.title: Procedure turn approach
items.lede: Reverse the aircraft heading within assigned airspace in order to align it with the final approach course. The procedure turn approach is an instrument maneuver used to reverse direction and establish the aircraft inbound on the intermediate or final approach course while insuring the remain within distance is observed. Procedure turns are depicted by a barb symbol on the approach plate, and the barb indicates which side of the outbound course to complete the turn.

items.title: Progressive spin

references.loc: Ch. 3 — Inadvertent Departure from Controlled Flight

items.lede: A progressive spin is what you get from reversing the rudder while holding full aft stick, the rudder half of the recovery without the stick half. The aircraft keeps rotating the original way for another turn and a half to two turns, and then spins the other way.

items.title: Propeller malfunctions

numbers.label: Pull PROP SYS CB if NP stable below

references.loc: Ch. 3 — Uncommanded Power Changes/Loss of Power/Uncommanded Propeller Feather

items.lede: This procedure should be used whenever uncommanded power changes occur or the engine fails to produce expected power. These conditions may be caused by engine rollback due to PMU scheduling, based on actual or faulty inputs to the PMU; oil, engine or fuel system contamination; a propeller dump solenoid failure; or loss of oil pressure to the propeller pitch control mechanism from a momentary contact between the oil transfer sleeve and the propeller shaft, a prop-sleeve touchdown.

items.title: Radial-arc intercepts
items.lede: On some approaches, missed approaches and departure procedures, you will be required to transition from a radial onto an arc. In these situations a lead point will be calculated to determine when to start your turn off of the radial onto the arc.

items.title: Radial intercept procedures
items.lede: A radial intercept is a procedure used to position the aircraft on a nearby radial with a new course inbound or outbound when not over the station. Radial intercepts are performed in training to practice orientation around a NAVAID, and may be used when navigating on airways and during some instrument approaches. The objective is to establish an intercept heading that will result in an appropriate angle and rate of intercept to the new radial or course.

items.title: Radial rendezvous
items.lede: A Blind Rendezvous, referred to as a TACAN rendezvous in fleet aircraft, is a visual circular rendezvous employed to rendezvous a flight above the weather after takeoff, or during the mission if the flight is separated. It is normally executed in a left-hand turn tangent to the briefed fix at a specified airspeed, altitude, and direction. The fix will be a VFR ground reference, an FMS reference point, or a radial/DME fix.

items.title: Recommended altitudes

numbers.label: Down to
numbers.value: last mile at or above MDA

references.loc: §907 — Airport Surveillance Approach (ASR) and PAR Without Glideslope (PAR W/O GS)

items.lede: On a surveillance approach, altitudes issued at each mile based on the descent gradient established for the procedure, down to the last mile that is at or above the MDA. They are issued if the pilot requests them, and what they buy you is a stabilised descent rather than a dive to the MDA followed by a long level segment.

items.title: Route management
items.lede: The primary means of navigation used on Visual Navigation flights will be a combination of Dead Reckoning and pilotage. DR is a logical system in which time, velocity, and distance are combined to arrive at a position. Pilotage is flying by visual reference to features on the ground.

items.title: Runaway trim
items.lede: Whenever the trim interrupt button is being depressed, or when the trim disconnect switch is set to disconnect, all trim systems are disengaged and the TAD is disconnected. When an individual trim system circuit breaker is pulled, the respective trim system will be inoperative.

items.title: RVFAC for RNAV approaches

references.loc: Ch. 1 — Vectoring to Final Approach Fix (FAF)

items.lede: Air traffic control clearance to the FAF can be handled by converting the loaded approach into a straight-in approach. This is accomplished by direct-to navigation to intercept the inbound course to the FAF.

items.title: Radar vectors to final approach course

references.loc: §819 — Radar Vectors to Final Approach Course (RVFAC)

items.lede: Radar vectors to final approach course is a procedure used by approach control to increase the arrival rate of aircraft by providing vectors onto the final approach course through the most expeditious routes consistent with traffic situations. Although this routing does expedite arrival at your destination, it has one characteristic of which you should be aware: the lack of published minimum altitudes until joining a segment of a published approach.
terms: Radar vectors to final approach course

items.title: S-1 pattern
items.lede: Maintain heading and airspeed throughout a series of constant rate descents and climbs. This pattern is flown at 150 KIAS and on any numbered or cardinal heading. It consists of a timed 1000 FPM descent for 1000 feet, followed by a timed 1000 FPM climb for 1000 feet. This series, descent and climb, is performed twice.

items.title: Safety check and call

events.title: Familiarization Cockpit Procedures
events.label: safety check/call prior to cockpit entry and departing aircraft

references.loc: §2 — How to Use This Checklist Guide

items.lede: Respect the Seat. Ejection seat and canopy fracturing system safety is paramount during ground operations, and if unintentionally or improperly fired the results could be fatal. Never enter or exit the airplane without the ejection seat safety pins installed.
terms: safety check/call prior to cockpit entry and departing aircraft

items.title: SCATSAFE maneuver
items.lede: The SCATSAFE maneuver is designed to demonstrate various performance characteristics of the aircraft when in a near-stalled condition. This maneuver will be demonstrated by the instructor. Every takeoff and landing you make requires you to operate the aircraft at low airspeed.

items.title: Scheduling

references.loc: Ch. 1 §6 — Crew Day and Crew Rest
§2.1 — Crew Day / Crew Rest / Work Week Limitations

items.lede: Crew day begins with the first scheduled event or official duty and ends upon completion of the last scheduled syllabus event, to include associated debrief and paperwork. Crew rest begins at the time of that completion and ends at the beginning of the subsequent crew day. VT-27 and VT-28 each publish their own limits on both, and on what may be scheduled in a day.

items.title: Seat height and rudder pedal adjustment

events.title: CNAF M-3710.7 Level-A Mission Readiness Training
events.label: Seat height and rudder pedal adjustment

items.lede: Seat height is adjusted so that it allows a clear view of the HUD, instrument panel and master warning and caution annunciators, and the flight controls are then checked to verify full control range is available at the selected seat height. Rudder pedal position is adjusted on the same checklist, immediately after it.
terms: Seat height and rudder pedal adjustment

items.title: Section approach procedures
items.lede: The Section Approach is used to expedite the recovery or for mutual support during certain emergencies. The key to a good formation approach is for Lead to fly a smooth, accurate instrument or visual approach, and for Wing to be proactive about maintaining position and complying with signals. Wing should also be prepared to assume the responsibilities of Lead at any time.

items.title: Section PEL
items.lede: If the Lead aircraft experiences an emergency, a radio call should be made quickly to allow Wing to get separation in order to allow Lead to maneuver as needed. If Wing experiences an emergency, they must communicate their intent to take the lead, and a verbal lead change should be conducted as soon as possible. The new Wing will transition to the Perch Position, assist in clearing the flight path, and monitor the PEL aircraft's performance.

items.title: Section takeoff
items.lede: The section takeoff has many practical advantages. It is frequently used to expedite departures and alleviates the necessity for a rendezvous in poor weather conditions. Wing will fly formation from brake release to rotation and into the airborne phase. Early detection and correction for changes in relative motion are the keys to performing a good section takeoff.

items.title: Securing the rear cockpit for solo
items.lede: Two failure modes drive the whole checklist: something in the back interfering with the flight controls, and a system in the back that cannot be controlled from the front. Every warning in it belongs to one or the other.
terms: Securing the rear cockpit for solo

items.title: See and avoid principle
items.lede: See and avoid is a pilot's best defense against a midair collision. The causal factor most often cited in midair accident reports is failure of the pilot to see and avoid the other aircraft. In most cases at least one of the pilots could have seen the other aircraft in time to avoid the collision.

items.title: Shuttle descent
items.lede: Descending to a lower altitude while in holding, normally at ATC’s initiative. Several aircraft holding at one fix are stacked with at least 1000 feet between them, and the shuttle is how each one is moved down as the stack works off. It is a constant airspeed descent flown inside the pattern.

items.title: Slip
items.lede: A slip is an out-of-balance flight condition used to increase the sink rate and lose excess altitude while maintaining a constant airspeed and a specific track over the ground.

items.title: Slow flight
items.lede: The Slow Flight Maneuver is designed to develop your ability to fly the aircraft in a near-stalled condition. Every takeoff and landing you make requires you to operate the aircraft at low airspeed. During training, students are taught flight at minimum controllable airspeed so they may learn the effect that airspeed has on aircraft performance and controllability.

items.title: Smoke and fume elimination

references.loc: Ch. 3 — Smoke and Fume Elimination/Electrical Fire

items.lede: This procedure may be used in the event of smoke or fumes as a result of an electrical fire or contamination from the ECS system.

items.title: Snivels

references.loc: §2.1 — Crew Day / Crew Rest / Work Week Limitations

items.lede: A snivel is a request to be left off the flight schedule for a given day or period. It is submitted in T-SHARP a fixed number of business days before the day requested, so it reaches Student Control before the schedule that would carry the event is built.

items.title: Speed brake use as a section

events.title: Formation
events.label: speed brake use as a section

items.lede: During the recovery phase, Lead may elect to use the speed brake to increase descent rates or decelerate the formation. The speed brake is a drag device and is therefore less effective as the airspeed is reduced. Extending and retracting the speed brake will induce pitch changes that may need to be counteracted. It is imperative that Lead maintains a stable platform and is clear about the intended use of the speed brake to preclude any closure issues between Lead and Wing.
terms: Speed brake use as a section

items.title: Spin
items.lede: Two primary factors must be present for an aircraft to spin: stalled AOA and yaw, rotation about the vertical axis. The spin entry requires full back stick with ailerons neutral, fully deflected rudder, and PCL to idle. A spin progresses through three phases: post-stall gyrations, incipient spin, and steady state spin.

items.title: Split-S
items.lede: The Split-S combines the first half of an Aileron Roll with the last half of a Loop. The aircraft climbs during entry and descends during recovery, and the maneuver is complete when the aircraft returns to level flight. It provides a means of rapidly converting the potential energy of altitude into airspeed while reversing the direction of flight.

items.title: Standard course corrections
items.lede: Making in-flight corrections to course and time is simple; however, you must know how far off course you are before determining a correction. Making a correction without knowing your exact location typically results in greater error. The techniques, in order, are to aim for a feature in the distance that is on course, to use funneling features, and to use a Standard Closing Angle.

items.title: Standard instrument departure
items.lede: Standard instrument departures are air traffic control procedures printed in graphic form for pilot use. SIDs will provide obstruction clearance and a transition from the terminal area to the appropriate enroute structure and can be found in DOD FLIP approach plates.

items.title: Standard time corrections
items.lede: Timing corrections are simply a matter of changing your GS for a period of time or off-course maneuvering. Off-course maneuvering will change the distance you fly, which will affect your timing. The recommended methods are off-course maneuvering, the proportional method and the ten percent method.

items.title: Standard terminal arrival
items.lede: A Standard Terminal Arrival is an Air Traffic Control coded IFR arrival route established for application by arriving IFR aircraft destined for certain airports. RNAV STARs for arrivals serve the same purpose, but are only used by aircraft equipped with a Flight Management System. The purpose of both is to simplify clearance delivery procedures and facilitate transition between enroute and instrument approach procedures.

items.title: Station passage
items.lede: Station passage is defined as the moment the aircraft passes directly over or abeam the radio facility. VOR station passage is primarily noted on the CDI as the first positive change of the TO/FROM indicator to "FROM" on the CDI.

items.title: Steady-state spin recovery
items.lede: After completing approximately three turns, the spin will have entered a near steady-state condition. Recover from a steady state spin by using NATOPS erect spin recovery procedures.

items.title: Steep turns
items.lede: Maintain smooth, coordinated flight in turns to specific headings at steeper than normal bank angles. These turns will normally be practiced at 45 and 60 degrees of bank and 150 KIAS, but other airspeeds and angles of bank are permissible. Enter a steep turn in the same manner as a normal turn.

items.title: Stereo routes
items.lede: Local agreements between an airfield and the FAA that let controllers issue a clearance by name instead of reading out the whole route. You file the stereo route identifier, and the clearance comes back as that identifier rather than a string of fixes — which is why the identifier is worth knowing before you key the mic to copy.

items.title: Strange Field operations
items.lede: Away from home field there is no line crew, no maintenance and no duty office. Everything those people normally do becomes the aircraft commander’s, and the discussion is about what specifically that means: postflight and preflight inspections, physically securing the aircraft, and accounting for the fuel packet.

items.title: Strike of ground object

references.loc: Ch. 3 — Emergency Engine Shutdown on the Ground

items.lede: A prop strike is one of the conditions NATOPS lists for the Emergency Engine Shutdown On The Ground procedure, alongside an engine fire, a chip light, the aircraft appearing likely to depart the prepared surface, and any other serious ground emergency.

items.title: Takeoff flap landings
items.lede: The approach is a descending 180° balanced turn to final in the flaps Up, TO, or LDG configuration. In the takeoff flap configuration, add power as required to maintain 120 KIAS on Downwind, approximately 42% torque, and at the 180 lower the nose to the 115 KIAS approach attitude.

items.title: Teardrop approach
items.lede: A teardrop approach makes use of an outbound to inbound radial intercept maneuver to reverse course and establish the aircraft inbound on the intermediate or final approach course while insuring the remain within distance is observed. A non-depicted teardrop approach is an authorized variant to the procedure turn, and is flown by intercepting an outbound radial offset 20° to the protected barb side of the procedure turn final approach course.

items.title: Terminate
items.lede: Terminate is a radio call, normally initiated by the Flight Lead, to terminate an exercise or maneuvering. This differs from the knock-it-off call in that it is anticipated and expected, such as after cruise maneuvering. Wing will request, or Lead will direct, a terminate.

items.title: Three Cs
items.lede: The Three Cs are the setup every stall is entered from: configuration, checklist, clear area. They may be accomplished in any order, and are not required between individual maneuvers flown in a series.

items.title: Time on target
items.lede: The first step in preparing a route is to determine the end point or destination. For purposes of Primary navigation training, the final checkpoint is referred to as the target, and the required time of arrival at this final checkpoint is the Time on Target. In real world terms the target could consist of an enemy position, landing zone or drop zone.

items.title: Timed turns
items.lede: A timed turn, maintaining a specific rate of turn in degrees per second, to an assigned heading maintaining altitude and airspeed. During normal IFR flight, turns will generally be performed at either standard or half standard rate. The Standard Rate Turn is 3° per second, so a turn of 180° will take one minute and a 360° turn will take two minutes.

items.title: Tire failures

references.loc: Ch. 3 — Landing with Blown Main Tire

items.lede: It may not be obvious that a main tire is blown until well into the landing roll. First indications of a blown main tire may include a pull towards the failed tire, or a rumble or shudder which can be mistaken for nose wheel shimmy.

items.title: TMS
items.lede: The Training Management System is where syllabus events are scheduled and training records are kept. For simulator and flight events, specific brief and taxi times are programmed into TMS and accounted for on the flight schedule.

items.title: Tower visit
items.sourcingLead: The familiarization visit to the tower, scheduled if able on this event. Purely local — what the visit covers and when it happens is squadron and field specific.

items.title: Tracking
items.lede: Tracking is the process of flying direct to a station or waypoint, correcting for winds, such that the aircraft track over the ground is the most direct route. Maintain heading equal to course until deviation is noted on the CDI and bearing pointer, determine the general direction of the wind, turn to re-intercept the desired course, then select a heading that will hold the aircraft on course.

items.title: Trim
items.lede: The secondary flight controls are used for trimming and balancing the aircraft in flight and to reduce the force required to actuate the primary flight control surfaces. To trim, deflect the trim switch in the opposite direction as the applied flight control force until that force is relieved.

items.title: Trouble T
items.lede: An obstacle departure procedure that has been developed solely for obstacle avoidance will be indicated with the symbol T on IAP charts, departure procedure charts, ODP or standard instrument departure plates.

items.title: Turn pattern
items.lede: The Turn Pattern is a series of constant angle of bank turns while maintaining altitude and airspeed. It consists of two 30° angle of bank turns in opposite directions for 90° of heading change, two 45° angle of bank turns in opposite directions for 180° of heading change, and two 60° angle of bank turns in opposite directions for 360° of heading change.

items.title: UFCP failure
items.lede: Check the UFCP circuit breaker, reset it if it is open, and land as soon as practical. The discussion is about what the affected cockpit can no longer do, since the other cockpit’s panel is unaffected and the aircraft is entirely flyable.

items.title: Unauthorized solo maneuvers

references.loc: Ch. 1 §6 — Crew Day and Crew Rest

items.lede: Solos may not practice spins, stalls, simulated engine failures, PPELs, or any maneuver which has not been previously introduced.

items.lede: A loss of thrust caused by uncommanded propeller feathering may be the result of an errant electrical signal to the feather dump solenoid causing reduction in oil pressure to the propeller pitch control mechanism, or of a prop-sleeve touchdown.

items.title: Unintentional instrument flight
items.lede: Instrument conditions are to be avoided at all times on a solo, so getting into them is already an emergency. Fly the aircraft, get on the instruments, check your altitude, and get out of IMC the way you entered it: if you were climbing, descend.

items.title: VFR chart preparation
items.lede: Select the charts to be used for the flight and check the dates of expiration to make certain they are current. A general rule when preparing your chart is to minimize marking up the chart to avoid possibly obscuring potential needed information. Recommend all marks be done initially in pencil to allow easy correction. Ballpoint black ink can be used after all work is completed and proofread.

items.title: VFR field entry/departure (AIM)

references.loc: §608 — Traffic Advisory Practices at Airports Without Operating Control Towers
§607 — Approach Control Service for VFR Arriving Aircraft

items.lede: When operating at an airport where traffic control is being exercised by a control tower, pilots are required to maintain two-way radio contact with the tower while operating within the Class B, Class C, or Class D surface area unless the tower authorizes otherwise. At airports without an operating control tower, a segmented circle visual indicator system, if installed, is designed to provide traffic pattern information. The key to communicating at an airport without an operating control tower is selection of the correct common frequency.

items.title: Visual descent point
items.lede: Depending on the location of the MAP, the descent from the MDA often will have to be initiated prior to reaching the MAP in order to execute a normal, approximately 3°, descent to landing. This point is called the visual descent point. The VDP will often be published on the approach chart; if not depicted, it may be computed.

items.title: Visual signals
items.lede: Your visual or radio communications within the flight must be clear and timely to avoid confusion. The Wingman should have time to acknowledge the signal before Lead executes the maneuver. Visual signals will generally be given to Wing when in parade, and the signal set is Appendix B of the F FTI.

items.title: Visual straight-in

references.loc: Ch. 3 — Landing with Unsafe Gear Indications

items.lede: The approach used when a break is precluded or impractical: weather, traffic, local procedure, or an emergency. It is also what you will fly at any non-Navy field, so it is worth being as practised as the overhead.

items.title: V-n diagram
items.lede: The operating flight strength diagram: load factor against airspeed, bounding everything the aircraft is allowed to do. Two kinds of limit meet on it, the aerodynamic one, where the wing stalls before it can generate more G, and the structural one, where the airframe is the thing that gives. Where they cross is the maneuvering speed.

items.title: VOR approach procedures
items.lede: Getting established on a VOR final and flying it. The transition is one of the course reversals or a radar vector; the final segment is the same either way — 6 Ts at the FAF, a 120-knot descent, level at the MDA before the VDP, and the MAP. The error the whole thing guards against is arriving at the MDA too late to land from it.

items.title: Wave-off
items.lede: The wave-off is a set of standard procedures used to effect the safe discontinuation of an approach. A wave-off may be initiated by the pilot, or may be directed by an external source: RDO, wheels watch, wave-off lights, IP, tower, another aircraft. The reason for an externally directed wave-off may not be apparent to the pilot, but the wave-off is mandatory unless a greater emergency exists.

items.title: Weight and balance
items.lede: It is the pilot’s responsibility to operate the aircraft within the weight and balance limits, and there are three ways to establish that you are. Which one you use is a matter of what the configuration is: a standard load is a lookup, anything else is a calculation.

items.title: Wind shear recovery
items.lede: The recovery is one line: if wind shear is encountered during an approach for landing, execute a go-around or wave-off. The remainder of the item is recognition of the conditions and the precautions taken on takeoff and approach.

items.title: Wingman/flight leader responsibilities
items.lede: The Designated Flight Lead is an administrative position, that in Primary is the instructor pilot designated on the flight schedule by the commanding officer. The Designated Flight Lead is the pilot who is ultimately responsible for the mission objectives and the safe and orderly conduct of the flight, and may fly in either position during the conduct of the flight. The Formation Lead is a physical position that may change throughout the flight: the pilot at the controls who is flying the lead position and is responsible for immediate conduct of the flight.

items.title: Wingover

numbers.label: Maximum bank at the reference point

items.lede: The Wingover is a 180° reversal in the direction of flight accomplished by combining a smooth climbing turn for 90° with a smooth diving turn for 90°. Recovery should be on the same altitude and approximately the same airspeed at which the maneuver was started. It is a slow and gentle maneuver when properly executed, and no abrupt control movements are necessary.
